I’ve always been mindful about my health, but over the past few months, it’s become harder to ignore the weight gain I’m terrified of. I’m not where I used to be—I don’t feel light on my feet anymore—and I’ve cut out bread, rice, anything starchy, just to feel in control. Sometimes I skip dinner if I feel like I ate too much earlier, though my husband worries. I tell him I’m fine, that I just “feel better” this way.

I check myself constantly in mirrors, store windows—anything reflective. My hands go to my waist without thinking, measuring. Even when people say I look thin, I don’t feel it. I just can’t trust how I look. At work, interpreting for clients all day, I’m so aware of my body in motion—my arms, my shape moving through space. I worry they’re watching not just my signs, but *me*. I’ve started wearing looser clothes to feel less exposed, even in the summer.

I don’t know if it’s about weight exactly, or just… not feeling right in my skin. But I can’t stop focusing on it. I don’t know if I’m protecting my health or punishing myself. And I don’t know what would happen if I just… ate.
D021-D017_h001.question_a:
I’ve been trying to stay as thin as possible for years now, but lately it’s gotten worse. I’m terrified of gaining any weight—I check my body in the mirror constantly, pinching the skin around my waist, my hips. Even though my husband says I’m too thin and my clothes hang off me, I can still feel fat. I’ve cut out almost all carbohydrates and fats—no bread, rice, oils, nothing. I count every calorie and work out for hours using sign language drills as exercise, like practicing ASL fingerspelling continuously to burn more.  

I weigh myself every morning, and if the number goes up even a little, I restrict even more the next day. I’m scared that if I eat normally, I’ll lose control. My cycle has stopped for over a year, but I still feel like I need to lose more.  

People notice me focusing on my body a lot, but it’s really just about my weight and shape—how slim I can get, how small I can feel. It’s not about my face or skin or nose—it’s the size of my body that haunts me. I just want to be lighter.
D021-D017_h001.question_b:

As an interpreter, I’m always in front of people, signing, using my face and hands constantly—which is exactly what makes it so hard. I can’t stop staring at my reflection. My skin, my nose, the way my jawline looks from the side... I check mirrors, windows, any surface that shows my face. I’ve taken to wearing heavier makeup and avoiding certain lighting, even during sessions. I cancel assignments sometimes, saying I’m sick, but really I just can’t face being seen.

I’ve also gotten really strict about food—no carbs, almost no fats. I weigh myself twice a day. I know I’m thin—my husband keeps telling me I’ve lost too much—but the thought of gaining even a pound makes me panicked. But it’s not *just* the weight. If anything, it’s my face that consumes me. I’ve read about eating disorders, but I don’t feel like it’s only about being thin. It’s that I can’t stand how I look, especially my nose and skin texture. I pick at my face constantly, even though it leaves marks. The mirror feels like a trap—I can’t look, but I can’t stop.

I’ve always cared about staying healthy, but over the past few months, I’ve become more focused on what I eat—mainly avoiding things like bread, rice, or anything “heavy,” even if they’re part of a balanced meal. I know my coworkers notice. I bring salads every day, no dressing, and I skip lunch meetings because I can’t predict the food. 

I weigh myself every morning—sometimes more if I’ve eaten something I wasn’t planning to. Even a half-pound increase makes me anxious, like I’m losing control. I’m not sure how much I weigh exactly, but I know I’ve lost a few pounds recently, and honestly, I’d like to lose a bit more. My clothes are looser, which feels like progress.

I wouldn’t say I’m obsessed with my appearance, but I do check mirrors more than I used to—how I look from the side, whether anything looks “off.” It’s hard to explain. I just want to feel… right. I still go to work, see clients, do my job, but part of me is always tracking—food, weight, how I look. I don’t know if it’s becoming a problem, or if I’m just being careful.
D021-D017_h005.question_a:
I’ve always been health-conscious, but over the past year, I’ve really had to tighten control. As a social worker, I’m constantly supporting others through crises, but I feel like I’m falling apart inside. I can’t stop thinking about my weight—I check the scale three or four times a day, and if it goes up even half a pound, I skip meals the next day or do extra cardio. I’ve cut out carbs completely and barely eat fats anymore, even though my coworkers tell me I’ve gotten too thin. I know I’m underweight, but the thought of gaining even a little scares me to the core.  

My clothes hang off me now, and people keep asking if I’m okay, but they don’t get it—being thin is the only thing making me feel like I have any control. I don’t wear makeup or fix my hair because I’m not worried about my skin or how my nose looks. It’s my shape—the size of my hips, my stomach—that I can’t stop focusing on. I measure them every night. It’s not about looking “better” in a general sense. It’s about being smaller. Safe.
D021-D017_h005.question_b:
I’ve always been careful about eating healthy, but over the past few years, it’s gotten… intense. I’m a social worker, so I’m used to paying attention to details, but I can’t stop noticing flaws in my face—my nose, especially. It feels huge, even though no one else seems to notice. I spend hours in the mirror checking it, tweaking my skincare, trying different angles. I even cancel home visits if I feel like my skin looks uneven.  

I’ve cut out carbs and fats almost completely—anything that might cause bloating or make my face look puffy. I weigh myself multiple times a day. If the number goes up even half a pound, I panic and go for long walks or skip meals. But honestly, it’s not really about being thin—it’s that I can’t stand how I look. My weight’s dropped, sure, but the fear isn’t about gaining weight so much as my face changing, my skin breaking out, or people noticing what I see. I know logically I’m thin, maybe too thin, but that’s not what keeps me up at night. It’s the mirror.
